metadata.title: Cities Associated with the School of Salamanca and Its Scholars
metadata.coordinate_note: Coordinates are approximate city-center coordinates, intended for mapping rather than cadastral use.
metadata.classification_note: Categories distinguish direct institutional centers, major extensions, debate/political sites, biographical links, precursor contexts, and later reception of Salamanca/Vitorian/Suarezian scholasticism.

cities.short_description: Primary institutional nucleus of the School of Salamanca, centered on the University of Salamanca and the Dominican convent of San Esteban.
Important neighboring university center linked to several major Salamancan scholars and to the wider Iberian late-scholastic network.
Site of the 1550–1551 Valladolid debate over conquest, Indigenous rights, and legitimate dominion, closely tied to questions developed by the School of Salamanca.
One of the strongest Portuguese continuations of the Salamanca tradition, especially in canon law, moral theology, and second scholasticism.
Portuguese university center important to the later scholastic tradition; Molina taught theology here and Suárez received his doctorate here.
Atlantic commercial center where Salamancan moral theology was applied to trade, prices, money, contracts, and the ethics of imperial commerce.
Linked biographically and academically to Domingo de Soto and to the early teaching career of Francisco Suárez.
Secondary academic site associated especially with Francisco Suárez during the early stages of his teaching career.
Included principally for its biographical connection to Luis de Molina rather than as an institutional center of the School.
A peripheral rather than formative center, relevant through the royal court and the later circulation, consultation, publication, and reception of late-scholastic political and legal thought.
Probably the strongest American institutional center connected directly to Salamancan-trained scholars and the application of their ideas to New World legal, economic, and theological questions.
associated_scholars_etc: Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico

cities.short_description: Early Augustinian center of higher studies where Alonso de la Veracruz taught philosophy and theology, making it one of the clearest direct transplants of Salamanca-trained scholasticism to the Americas.
associated_scholars_etc: Augustinian house of studies at Tiripetío

cities.short_description: Part of the Michoacán intellectual and missionary environment in which Salamanca-derived arguments about Indigenous communities, property, governance, and evangelization were put into practice.
Major South American center of scholastic theology, canon law, natural law, and debates over colonial rule through San Marcos and the city's religious colleges.
A crucial precursor to Salamanca's American debates: Dominican denunciations of abuses against Indigenous peoples here helped frame questions later systematized by Vitoria and his successors.
Episcopal seat of Bartolomé de las Casas and an important setting for practical disputes over Indigenous freedom, forced labor, evangelization, and legitimate colonial authority.
Important colonial university and Jesuit center where Vitorian and especially Suárezian scholastic traditions were transmitted and adapted in the northern Andes.

cities.former_name: La Plata de la Nueva Toledo / La Plata / Chuquisaca
cities.short_description: Major legal, ecclesiastical, and university center of the Audiencia of Charcas where late-scholastic natural-law and political thought became part of colonial learned culture.
associated_scholars_etc: University of San Francisco Xavier of Chuquisaca

cities.former_name: Santa Fe / Santa Fe de Bogotá
cities.short_description: Colonial academic center in New Granada where Vitorian, Thomist, and Suárezian natural-law traditions circulated through universities and religious colleges.
associated_scholars_etc: Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario

cities.former_name: Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala
cities.classification_category: American secondary reception and reform context
cities.short_description: Colonial capital connected to Dominican reform activity, debates over Indigenous peoples, and the later university transmission of Iberian scholastic thought in Central America.
associated_scholars_etc: University of San Carlos of Guatemala

cities.short_description: Important later colonial university center where Jesuit education transmitted Suárezian and broader second-scholastic philosophy, theology, and political thought in the Río de la Plata region.
